ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, in the Cartesian coordinate system, the point $A(3, 3)$ forms a rhombus $AOBC$ with $OA$ as one of its sides. What are the coordinates of point $C$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Let's draw AE$\perp$x-axis at E, and CF$\perp$x-axis at F,\\
then quadrilateral AEFC is a rectangle,\\
$\therefore$AE=CF, and AC=EF,\\
$\because$ point A is (3, 3),\\
$\therefore$AE=OE=3,\\
$\therefore$OA=$3\sqrt{2}$,\\
$\because$ quadrilateral AOBC is a rhombus,\\
$\therefore$AC=OA=$3\sqrt{2}$,\\
$\therefore$CF=AE=3, and OF=3+$3\sqrt{2}$,\\
$\therefore$ the coordinates of point C are (3+$3\sqrt{2}$, 3),\\
so, the answer is: The coordinates of point C are $\boxed{(3+3\sqrt{2}, 3)}$.

ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the figure: from the attached figure it can be seen that O is the coordinate origin, the x-axis is horizontal to the right, and the y-axis is vertical upward; line segment OA goes from O obliquely upward to the right to point A; point B is on the positive x-axis; point C is to the right of A, AC is a horizontal line segment, and AOBC is drawn as a rhombus in the shape of a parallelogram, with AC parallel to OB. Then reason: it is known that A=(3,3), so vector OA=(3,3), length |OA|=sqrt(3^2+3^2)=3sqrt(2). Because AOBC is a rhombus, all sides are equal, so OB=OA=3sqrt(2). Also because OB is on the positive x-axis, vector OB=(3sqrt(2),0), point B=(3sqrt(2),0). In the rhombus, that is, the parallelogram AOBC, vector AC equals vector OB, therefore C=A+OB=(3,3)+(3sqrt(2),0)=(3+3sqrt(2),3).
